speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 16 at the conclusion of the debate which followed the motion of the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) I told the house of various policies which were being adopted in an effort to stimulate the production of fuel. As there appears to be some confusion as to the application of the subsidy on fuel wood I should like to elaborate on my previous statement, particularly to define clearly what is meant by a dealer. I think it possible that my reply to a question from the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) which appears at page 1317 of Hansard may have given rise to some misunderstanding.
A subsidy of $1 per standard cord of 128 stacked cubic feet will be paid to wood fuel dealers on all commercial wood fuel contracted for and cut on or before June 30, 1943, and held to dealers' account on that date. In recommending dealers, the office of the fuel controller will be guided by the following definition of the persons and fuel eligible for the bonus:
1.	The coal controller will have authority in his discretion to recognize as a dealer any person who was a dealer in wood fuel and who held a wartime prices and trade board licence as of March 5, 1943.
2.	The coal controller will have authority to recognize as dealers those holding licences granted since March 5, 1943, in special cases where, because of a real contribution to increased wood fuel supply, it would be in the public interest to take such action. All such special cases will require approval from the controller's office at Ottawa.
Fuel Shortage

Replying to a question by the hon. member for Souris, I said this:
If the man in question cuts one hundred cords of wood and sells it himself, he is a dealer and would be entitled to the bonus as a dealer.
The special circumstances of a transaction of that kind would be inquired into by the coal controller. The coal controller would of course eliminate cross-transactions between farmers, and any transactions outside of those by bona fide dealers in wood fuel.

The other day when tne fuel problem was being discussed in the house I referred to circumstances under which wood fuel was cut by community effort. The farmer allowed the people to come in to cut fuel, and for every cord they cut he received one cord for himself; thus the people who did the cutting were able to get sufficient fuel for themselves. They paid all the costs of the saw, and so forth. This meant of course that the farmer's wood bush was depreciated; would he not be entitled to the dollar subsidy on the quantity which went to the village? He is actually not a dealer; it is a community effort.

The transaction in question would be one of those the regulations are planned to prevent. The man neither cut the wood nor delivered it as a dealer. He sold standing wood and was paid in wood. He must be a bona fide dealer; his effort must be different from the ordinary effort of settlers who ordinarily cut wood for their own use.

Will this
apply to wood cut by mills more or less as a by-product? The minister is reported on .page 1315 of Hansard as follows:
It is to pay a bonus of $1 a cord for wood cut before June 1 and in the hands of dealers on that date.
There appears to be a conflict as to the date; in another place it is given as June 30.
June 1 is the date. It does not matter who cuts the wood; if it is in a dealer's hands on the first day of June and offered for sale to the public, the dealer will get the bonus of $1 per cord.
Does it apply to wood cut by mills as a by-product and sold as fuel?
Yes.

If there is a cooperative enterprise by which a number of persons gather together, purchase a wood lot and cut wood for their own particular town or village, would the dollar a cord subsidy apply in that case?
Only if the wood is delivered to a dealer for sale to the public at large, not for sale back to the people who cut it. A man who cuts wood for his own use is not entitled to the bonus.

In my constituency
probably sixty per cent of the wood is cut by farmers and sold direct to the users. Would the farmers get the bonus?

A farmer selling direct to a user gets the ceiling price for his wood, whereas a farmer selling to a dealer gets the dealer's price, and the dealer makes his profit. A man who cuts wood and sells direct to a user would not be entitled to the $1 per cord, unless he stocks it and sells it to the public.
Would a farmer cutting 100 to 200 cords of wood get the subsidy?

The subsidy is paid to
dealers. If a farmer can qualify as a dealer to the satisfaction of the fuel controller he will get the subsidy. If he simply sells to one customer or two customers, he will not get it. He must be a dealer stocking wood and offering it for sale to the public. If he is simply cutting a supply for a customer, he does not qualify.
I understand the idea of the bonus or the subsidy is to obtain greater production. If the producer does not get the bonus, how will you get more production?
I think I have explained that.

For a copy of all letters, telegrams, correspondence, and other documents received by the Minister of Labour or by Mr. MacNamara, in answer to mobilization act interpretative letter No. 1, dated February, 1943.

Prefacing my question with the remark that it is a happy position to be in, as described by the minister a few moments ago, that one in the opposition assumes such tremendous control over the house, even for one afternoon, I should like a little information from the minister.
This interim supply, as I understand it, is a matter of providing before the main estimates have been passed for contingencies which arise in connection with the government services for a short time. I should like to know why, in view of the fact that in all probability we shall be in session for some considerable time, the minister would not ask for one-twelfth of the amount, rather than one-sixth, as has been suggested by the chairman.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, it is a matter of saving the time of the house. If I remember correctly, last year I estimated for one-sixth and was granted one-twelfth only. "Granted" is the correct word, because this is an occasion on which I simply have to ask the opposition for what they will let me have. But all that happens in a case of the kind is that about a month later we have to go over it again, and I do not see any advantage in doing that; it means that at some time there will be two or three hours' discussion without anything being accomplished. The supply is always granted. It does give an opportunity for a little crossargument which otherwise would not take place. But I am sure there is no possibility of getting all the main estimates passed before the end of two months; and I suggest that if we want to economize the time of the house, the granting of one-sixth supply would be more desirable than the granting of one-twelfth.

Is there any special
reason why we should depart this session from the plan and the procedure which we adopted on a prior occasion?

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: INTERIM SUPPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before second
reading is given I would ask the minister to indicate to the house, if he has the information before him, the increases in the general non-war estimates for the year 1943-44. On another occasion during a previous debate in this house the minister made some reference to those estimates, but before this supply is granted I think we should have from the minister a statement giving the information in greater detail. There is a feeling which I think is widespread throughout the dominion that while loans and taxation to raise funds for war purposes should receive every support, sometimes the money raised by such loans or taxation does not all go into actual war expenditures, and the public are not inclined to regard the ordinary peace-time estimates in the way they regard expenditures which are closely connected with the war effort.
There is a responsibility upon the minister and the government to indicate to the people that so far as lies within their power strict economy shall be practised, particularly in regard to the non-war groups which from time to time appear in the estimates. This does not mean that there should be any let-up in the economy that is applied1 to war expenditures, but there is a disposition on the part of the public to be even more careful about what the government is doing, to make sure that expenditures which have to do with matters not directly connected with the war are not being increased. I am not so sure that the statement made by the minister on a previous occasion sufficiently explained the stand of the government in that regard, because large numbers of our people to-day are exerting every effort to cooperate with and help the government in every possible way, by giving

Interim Supply Bill
them all the money possible with which to carry on this great war for our treasured way of life. But hon. members of this house who are closely in touch with the people will corroborate my statement that they are watching the government very closely, particularly in regard to what has been done in the way of economy with respect to peace-time estimates. Time after time, eloquently and to the best of his ability and capacity, the minister has told the people of Canada that they must forgo many of the things they would1 be enjoying if we were in the midst of peace. The minister has taken that stand, no doubt with the full support of the government of the day. In effect he asked the people to tighten their belts during this period of war; to use the words of the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris), the people have been asked to end this carnival spirit, to cease all unnecessary expenditures, to direct all their energies to the winning of' the war, and to give where they can and to the last cent. Once that policy -was announced by the Minister of Finance the responsibility of the government became even greater to see that the government itself should do the same thing, because nothing is more necessary than that governments as well as individuals should practise what they preach. I have given some indication of what the government has been preaching from one end of Canada to the other, and now I ask the minister to give us some indication of what the government is practising.
I realize that this year the non-war estimates are considerably higher than they have been in previous years. I listened to the minister's explanation of a portion of that increase, but I suggest to him that indications have come to light here and there of a lack of economy throughout the administration. It is not always possible for members of parliament, in the limited time at their disposal, no matter how conscientious they may be, or how anxious they may be to do so, to find out whether or not war economies are being practised. Now, however, we have before us the non-war estimates, and in view of the little information that has come to light from time to. time with respect to lack of economy in these departments, the minister ought to make a statement this afternoon, and I ask him' to do so, to indicate just what has been done since the close of the last session of parliament to effect economies in peace-time operations of the various departments of government. I do not suggest that these should be ordinary economies, because the minister has not asked the people of Canada to exercise just ordinary economy; he has asked the people to go much farther; he has asked them to go the limit. I do not think we are asking too much when we suggest the minister should give a statement in regard to these non-war expenditures. We will deal with the war-time expenditures when the time comes; for it would not be proper to deal with them now. But the Minister of Finance must satisfy this house, and the country, on this the first occasion on which the estimates for the ensuing year are before us, that the government is exercising not an ordinary but an1 extraordinary economy, and that not a dollar is being wasted in these departments.

I should like to say a word following the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) in this regard. I know the country does look to the government and to this house to see that there are no wasteful expenditures. But to my mind economy is of two kinds. There is wasteful expenditure, and there is the economy which comes sometimes from worthwhile expenditure. We have to be careful even in war-time that we do not cut down the ordinary services of the country to the extent that we penalize necessitous people and lose the benefit of services which we have built up over a period of time. While I am sympathetic with the suggestion of the leader of the opposition that the minister should lay before the house any steps that have been taken to bring about worth-while economies, I should not like it to go abroad that this house considers that in this time of war some of our services that have been instituted over a period of years should be reduced to the

Interim Supply Bill
extent of becoming worthless or practically so, to the people. I am thinking at the moment largely of the social services of some of the provinces, where already there have been reductions in the amounts paid to old age pensioners, and expenditures of the kind. I am thinking also of some of our own employees, who, notwithstanding the higher cost of living, are still receiving a remuneration which is entirely inadequate. I learned not long ago that at the Indian Head forestry farm, where we employ seasonal help, married men who have to maintain homes and provide themselves with work clothes and heavy gloves to handle the shrubs and trees are being paid twenty-seven cents an hour, which is altogether out of proportion to the present cost of living.
We have departments such as mines and resources, which should be going forward with their work so that we may be laying plans for the public use of our natural resources when the war ends. Indeed I think that one of the real economies-the house knows that the group with which I am associated believe the same thing-would be the public development of some of our great natural resources.
A short time ago I had the opportunity of hearing an outstanding man in the city of New York say that we have in this country undeveloped in this time of war a source of oil that would be of immeasurable benefit. He quoted from one who is an authority in the field of oil. Afterwards I secured the series of lectures delivered by Mr. Wallace E. Pratt, an outstanding geologist, formerly chief director of mines bureau of science, in the United States and now an executive director of the most powerful oil corporation in the world, Standard Oil of New Jersey. I should like to see public exploration and development carried on so that we can economize in a real way in obtaining revenue. I happen to have that series of lectures in my hand and I should like to read one paragraph, as follows:
Challenging, also, to the oil man is the occurrence of the Athabaska tar sands, spreading over thousands of square miles of the central portion of the Williston basin.
Stretching away down beyond the Dakotas.
These so-called tar sands display a volume of oil greater than any other so far discovered on earth. Well considered estimates place the volume of the oil-equivalent of the Athabaska tar sands at from 100 to 250 billion barrels; yet the total discoveries of all time over all of the earth, as we have already noted, do not exceed 81 billion barrels. Moreover, the Athabaska tar sands are not a variety of oil shale as has been commonly assumed; they are literally oil-saturated sands. All the shales contain a kerogen-like compound which, like coal, can be converted into oil through retorting 
under appropriate pressure-temperature conditions. But the Athabaska tar sands contain oil itself. At the surface to be sure the oil is waxy and inspissated but underground, down-dip from the outcrop, the tar sands yield a heavy oil through wells. There is little doubt that as a source of oil they could be exploited commercially to-day; eventually they may well come to be looked upon as one of the important energy resources of North America.
Those are the words of a man who has spent his lifetime in oilfield exploration. A real economy at this time might be the expenditure of public money for the exploration and prospecting of natural resources that we might put to good use now in wartime. Let me caution the house that if we give away these great natural resources as we have been doing and are doing to-day under war conditions we shall rue it. It is not only the lending of money to the Aluminum Corporation to which I particularly object, but the alienation in perpetuity of one of the greatest waterpower resources of the world.
Every attempt should be made to economize where economy is possible. Hon. members know that there are places where expenditures could be cut to some extent-advertising, for example. I saw an advertisement the other day with regard to hogs; it was meant entirely for slaugther-houses, but it was published in papers all across the country instead of in the trade papers where the three or four hundred operators of abbatoirs would see it. There is-also the quantity of literature, both mimeographed and printed, that comes to our offices from government departments. Certainly there are places where there can be economies. But what I am particularly interested in is that we shall not practise false economy. Sometimes expenditures of money on projects such as I have outlined, and particularly at this time when we are preparing for the aftermath of this great war, are justified and might be productive of great good in the future.
So that while I support what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) has said, I wanted also to place before the house what I might term a word of caution in respect of economies. Economies of the right kind are beneficial, but economies of the wrong sort may do harm to services we have built up,, and to extensions of our public endeavours that ought to be made both now and in the period which follows the war.

Interim, Supply Bill

Getting down to rock bottom, the philosophy of this group is one of spending rather than of saving. It is the philosophy of spending something into existence, rather than that of saving and putting it into existence by way of debt.
There is a difference, however, between the economy of money and the economy of materials. Of course in war time the whole country is called upon to make sacrifices. We must make sacrifices in war time; we recognize that. Our whole national economy must be brought into line with the best possible war effort, and that means sacrifice. But it is a wrong principle to have an economy under which our people must sacrifice miserably; they can make sacrifices, and still do it happily. We can bear our burdens, but the people are not going to bear unnecessary burdens.
Let me say a word or two with reference to the psychology of waste. It is one thing to waste our money by excessive expenditures. It is another thing entirely to waste the materials we must have for an effective war effort. This psychology in the minds of the people can either be a tremendous help to our war effort or a tremendous hindrance to it. We call upon our people to save, to cut to the bone. But when they see waste they are not going to make sacrifices happily.
In the past I have had amazing things brought to my attention. Some of them I should not care to bring to the attention of the government from the floor of the house, because I should not want to embarrass the government to that extent. The conditions I have in mind may not be entirely their fault. Some of them are of local application, and it may be best that they remain so. But these are conditions which do not help the public to make sacrifices happily for the war effort.
For instance in some respects there is a wastage of gasoline. The waste may not be great, but I approach the subject from the point of view of its psychological effect on the thinking of our people. Men have told me that when the spout of a gasoline tank is transferred from one aeroplane to another it is sometimes not shut off, with the result that gallons of gasoline are sprinkled on the ground. While it may be a small wastage, and while it may be said that one should not take up the time of the house in discussing it the fact remains that people see these things happening.
I was told of a farmer on whose field an aeroplane had crashed. When he went to -he scene of the crash he saw oil dropping on
the ground. He asked permission to buy the oil, and the reply was, "Oh, no, we cannot sell you that oil; we have no authority to do so." I suppose there was some red tape involved. He dismissed the matter from his mind. But the next day after the wreckage had been hauled away he found that a small area of ground on which the oil had fallen was spoiled. What was the reaction in that man's mind? He said to me, "I should have liked to get it for nothing, but I offered to buy it. I could not buy it, and now it lies on the ground, wasted." A few square yards of ground were spoiled. True, it was not a very large area, but the point is that there was wastage.
That is the type of waste we do not want. Every man of us, whether he be in the services, in business, on the farm or in the street, must strive to cut down that kind of waste. We must help to bring that about through our contacts with our people.
So far as money wastage is concerned I would point out that we have two committees in parliament who are working on this matter. The duty of the committee on war expenditures is to investigate every type of war expenditure in which they believe they can discover any waste, and it is their duty to recommend to the government where expenditures can be cut. The scope of the committee is huge, including everything from salt on the soldier's table to battleships. I do not know how that committee can complete its work. It should be sitting nearly every day, deciding as to where we can best effect economies.
The public accounts committee, one of our standing committees, has had certain specific items referred to it for investigation. These committees can deal with expenditures of money, and I am satisfied to leave that work in their hands, in the belief that it will be done thoroughly. I join with the leader of the opposition and the leader of. the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in asking that unnecessary expenditures be cut down. Government waste should be looked into carefully. Let us not waste one single particle of material which can be used in our war effort.

I do not wish to speak at any length at this time, but I feel that in connection with the voting of an amount such as is being asked for by the Minister of Finance, we as an opposition have a tremendous responsibility to discharge in scrutinizing with care and attention the expenditures that are. being made. We realize that, during war time, on occasion the necessity for speed brings about extravagance and extra cost.	Our attitude	as an
opposition has been to cooperate with the government, but since the beginning of this war I do not know that I have ever heard any minister of the crown admit in the house that in the main the attitude of this opposition has been to criticize where necessary but to cooperate to t'he one end of winning the war. If that attitude were adopted by the government, it would make a great deal of difference in the expedition of the business of the house and, in particular, in the assistance which might be rendered to the government by the opposition.
Here we have a tremendous amount of money to be voted. There is not one member of this committee other than the minister who has any idea whatever how it is to be expended, except in bulk as broken down by the figures of March 3. All we have is a record of large amounts. The attitude of the government in thie last year and a half has been steadily that of failing in greater and greater measure to give such details to parliament as would make possible fair and careful scrutiny and examination.
There are only two ways in which we can assist in. assuring the people of Canada that expenditures are being made properly. The first is, say in connection with the Department of Munitions and Supply-I see the minister is in his place-that there should be publication of contracts let by that department. The next point is that there has been a tendency on the part of the government during the last year to rely more and more on the

War Appropriation
answer that "it is not in the public interest."
I was reading to-day excerpts from "Parliamentary Grants" by Durell, in which he sets forth the duty of an opposition as far as supply is concerned. At page 473 this very apt statement is made:
By many individuals the possession of public money is regarded merely as a trust which they will have fully discharged when they have spent their funds on utilitarian objects, and laid them out in the manner vdiich they consider best in the interests of the public service. This idea is prevalent even in peace time. In war the danger is enormously increased not only among those who are for the first time placed in charge of public moneys, but even among those who have had a peace training, but are inclined to think that a state of war automatically removes all financial restrictions.
Then he goes on to say that in time of war one of the most necessary safeguards, having in mind the protection of the public interest, is that the people who deal with the government must realize that the transactions they enter into are open to public scrutiny at all times. And he says:-
A reckoning will be demanded, though the recollection that this is so is likely to be swamped by the flood of money which is being poured out.
The mere availability of vast sums of money, which is a necessary accompaniment of war, is no excuse for greater expenditure than is necessary for the fulfilment of military requirements.
But war inculcates what Gladstone calls "the spirit of expenditure", and the availability increases the temptation to spend, and such temptation increases in proportion as the possibility of a reckoning appears to be distant or unlikely to be strict.
In time of war there should be reasonably strict accountability. How can there be that accountability when none of us knows what contracts the government has entered into?
It is time we have an opportunity to ask questions. But those questions will be merely in the nature of fishing expeditions unless we have information as to the contracts that have been awarded or entered into.
We are approaching another victory loan campaign. All of us wish to see the campaign a success. A few months ago when the minister was about to make an important announcement over the radio to the Canadian people he gave advance warning and we were all listening. No more useful piece of work could be done by the Minister of Finance to-day than to go on the radio and ask the people of Canada for their cooperation, ask them to bring to the attention of the government any instances of extravagance or waste that they know of, giving assurance that when that information is brought to the attention of the government that appropriate action will be taken-I have no doubt there would be an avalanche of it-

By following this suggestion you will have the people of Canada believing that an effort is being made by all of us in this house to ensure that reckless and improper expenditures shall not be condoned by this parliament. It is a very simple suggestion; but if the minister follows it, men and women from one end of Canada to the other, in village, town, city and in the country, who know of instances, or at least believe they do, in which there has been overexpenditure would feel that now the government will take the matter in hand, and that their money will be utilized so as to secure the greatest possible return in helping to win the war.
What has been the attitude of the government in recent weeks? Too frequently they are hiding behind the answer, "It is not in the public interest". Let me mention several specific instances. I have had Hansard examined for the purpose, and I find that, generally speaking, in 1940 and 1941 the occasions when the answer, "It is not in the public interest" was given were fair and reasonable, and that the national interest in war time was the prime consideration. There were two examples that were rather difficult to understand. On March 17, 194)1, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) asked for certain information in regard to incomes in Canada. His question, as reported at page 1565 of Hansard of that date, reads:
How many individuals in Canada are in receipt of incomes, as shown by the income tax returns filed in 1940, (a) $10,000 to $25,000; (b) $25,000 to $50,000; (c) $50,000 to $100,000; (d) in excess of $100,000?
An answer was given in regard to the first two groups, but regarding the last two it was said that it was not deemed in the public, interest to answer these separately.
There may have been some reason for that answer, but it is rather difficult to understand it.
On April 2, 1941, a perfectly reasonable question was asked the Minister of Munitions and1 Supply (Mr. Howe) by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy). The question was whether or not the government had purchased, directly or indirectly, a vessel named the Winchester. The second part read:
2. If so, (a) from whom; (b) upon whose recommendation; (c) at what price; (d) where *was delivery made?
Why should this information not be given? Yet the answer given was:
It is not in the public interest to give details of this purchase.

This is the type of answer which arouses a degree of suspicion which may or may not be warranted.
In 1942, generally speaking, the occasions on which the answer "not in the public interest" was given appear understandable, with two exceptions. On April 23, 1942, the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. Hazen) asked:
1.	What are the names and addresses of the persons to whom cheques were issued (a) for over $10,000, (b) for $5,000 to $10,000 on wheat acreage reduction bonus?

The answer was that it was not in the public interest to give the information. Since when has it not been in the public interest for the people of Canada to be told how their money is being expended? Why should those *of us who ask these questions be denied information which by no stretch of the imagination could be of assistance to the *enemy?
In 1942 several of this kind were given, to none of which I take particular objection. But in the last few weeks the trend has been toward denying the members of the house information to which they are entitled. I point to an answer given on March 1, 1943, when the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) moved:
For a copy of specifications and plans of the proposed permanent houses to be built by Wartime Housing Limited at Hamilton, Ontario.

The minister went still further. On February 15 he was asked this question, at page 392 of Hansard:

2.	Has the government employed the services of chartered accountants to inquire into the operations of such companies?

The answer given by the minister to the first two questions was, yes, and to the third:

Justifiable it may have been to answer that it was not in the public interest to give the information when an investigation was in the hands of the mounted police. But the answer the minister gives to the last question will fortify those who are wrongdoers in the belief that under no circumstances may parliament secure information respecting irregularities committed by them. If there is one way to prevent irregularity it is to see to it that those who do wrong shall know that parliament will be granted every opportunity by the government to ascertain the wrongdoing and to demand that it be properly punished. When an answer is given by the government that it is not in the public interest, that is the end so far as parliament is concerned. Your Honour gave a ruling last year, as reported on page 1976 of Hansard, as follows:
I have pointed out already that Bourinot states that an answer to a question cannot be
insisted upon if the answer be refused by a minister on the ground of the public interest, nor can the question be replaced upon the order paper after a refusal by a minister to answer, nor can the refusal of the minister to answer be raised as a question of privilege.
That shows how carefully a minister should consider the matter before giving an answer that denies information to an hon. member of this house. One thing I have noticed in travelling throughout the country is that men and women are asking us who are in parliament, "What are you doing to check wasteful expenditures?" That is why I make this plea to the Minister of Finance, whose courage I admire and whose industry merits the praise of all. If he would give the assurance I have suggested it would result in a feeling of determination on the part of the people and, what is more, a new incentive to them to give all that they have to the country at this time.
I consider it	my	duty	as a	member ofthis house to point out that in the last loan campaign the argument was raised all. too often as an answer for not contributing that the government was not demanding the discontinuance of overexpenditure and extravagance. I realize that in the vast amounts that are being spent there will be expenditures here and there which may be extravagant, but the people should know that those who overexpend, those	who	take	advantage of thegovernment, if	you	will,	those	who realizelarger profits than- any person in time of war has a right to realize, will be proceeded against. Wherever there is a suggestion of overexpenditure the names of the wrongdoers must be brought to the light of day in parliament,	and	they	must	be made to
disgorge all they have wrongfully taken from the state.
There is nothing partisan in this suggestion. It is simply an appeal to the minister, and I ask members on all sides of the house to support it. If it is acceded to it will give new hope to the Canadian people. The minister and the Prime Minister are the only two men who can do this. I am asking in all sincerity that the suggestion be not brushed aside, that it be accepted. If that is done, when the next victory loan comes around the results will be more than can otherwise be expected. If that is done, I will do what I did in the last campaign, and what I believe all hon. members did-I will give of my time and energy to the utmost. I shall then be able to go to the people and say that the rumours they have heard have been investigated and have been found to be false, or have been found to be true and the wrong-

doers have been punished. If that is done, the response to the next victory loan will be greater than ever before. Show the people that where waste and overexpenditure can be prevented, it will be prevented and punished, and we shall have done much to improve the determination and morale of the Canadian people.

I think that what I am saying is within the resolution, Mr. Chairman.
I do not think the minister will dispute that agriculture is one of the most important munitions of war. It is one of the most vital undertakings on the north American continent for the welfare of the united nations. The figures given by the Minister of Agriculture, to which the Minister of Finance has referred, call for an immensely increased production over previous years. Yet the farmers have lost some 400,000 men to war industries and the armed forces, and I do not see how we can obtain the results desired by the government and the people if something is not done' about it.
There is just one other matter I shall refer to, namely, coarse grains, as to which I obtained an answer the other day. These come under the price ceiling, and the exporter who exports grain to-day receives a nice profit over the price allowed to produce under our price ceiling. I think something should be done bv the government to see that the producer gets this profit rather than the exporter. It is but another example of the unfairness of the present controls.
As to waste, I think there is evidence of it in many places. The other day a return was brought down showing that 100,000 men had been discharged from the armed forces. I am glad to see the Minister of National Defence in his seat, because I am satisfied that that is altogether too great a percentage, having regard to the fact that the Canadian army has not yet been in battle. To enlist and equip these 100,000 soldiers at approximately $200 apiece would cost $20,000,000. I imagine that these men would serve on the average not less than six months, and that would be another $20,000,000. There is at least $40,000,000, which in my opinion is a direct waste of public money. For the benefit of the
Minister of Pensions and National Health let me say, by way of contrast that I do not think some of these men are given enough money to spend for the purpose of clothing and rehabilitating themselves upon their discharge. The Minister of National Defence should explain to the house why there is such a large percentage of discharges from the armed forces. The percentage is altogether too great, and it costs this country too much money. I want to be clear on this point. I am satisfied that no taxpayer begrudges a single dollar that is spent to see to it that our army is the finest and best equipped in the world, but the taxpayers do begrudge these wastes that are taking place.
There are many other wastes. Take for, instanoe the wartime information board, about which a return was brought down to the house the other day. It showed that since the middle of last summer the board has cost us over half a million dollars, and that we have 134 publicity men, 25 of whom have salaries exceeding $3,000. It is interesting to note what the status of some of these people was in the newspaper business before they received these appointments and the salaries that go with them.
There has been built up in this country what I think cannot be called anything but a bureaucracy. You might term these controllers the white collared army of this country. I know that many of them are giving splendid service and are probably receiving less money than they made in their own private business. But many of them are enjoying a larger salary than they ever obtained before, and I doubt whether very many of them are returning anything in the way of war effort to the country. The Minister of Finance should assure the nation that these wastes will be eliminated. The people are prepared to lend and give all they can to the war effort because they know that everything is at stake. But the Minister of Finance, above all other members of the government, must assure the people that these wastes which are taking place under their own eyes out in their own communities will be eliminated. Then the people will be prepared to go without some of the luxuries of life and in some cases without some of the necessities to assist in putting over the loan. As was stated by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), I am satisfied that every member of this group will do all he can to help in putting the coming loan over the top, as we have done in the past. But let me repeat that the Minister of Finance and the other

War Appropriation

ministers must assure the people that these wastes that are taking place will be eliminated. Otherwise the loan may not be the success we hope for.

speechtext:
We are dealing briefly with an appropriation of $648 millions, and in view of the fact that before long we shall be embarking upon another victory loan drive, perhaps I may be able to contribute something to the ' debate by suggesting to the various ministers, particularly the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Munitions and Supply, and possibly the Minister of Labour, the advisability at an early day, before the launching of the victory loan campaign, of giving a

statement to the house on two or three matters which are uppermost in the minds of the people in relation to our war effort.
In the last couple of months there has been considerable criticism and discussion in the daily press and throughout the country concerning the prevalence of so much absenteeism in industry, and why it is so difficult to get men who are working in our war industries, and in our peace industries as well, to put into production the effort by w'ay of overtime which is absolutely necessary. The situation is so serious that a statement as to what remedy the ministers in charge of the various departments have to propose would be appropriate at this time.
Now that the war is in its third or fourth year, the time has come when we should be pretty well over the period of slow-downs in industry caused by plants being converted from one type of production to another, or being tooled and set up for one particular type of production, where companies have large staffs of men but not sufficient orders, plans or material to continue in orderly production and keep their payrolls intact. The time has come when the public has reason to expect a more definite statement as to *what is the actual condition in industry in regard to slow-downs by the men employed therein and the consequent reduced production which inevitably results in increased costs and causes dissatisfaction with labour.
We are approaching the Easter recess, before we get into a full discussion of munitions and supply production, and particularly before the victory loan campaign is launched, there should be given to the Canadian people a statement indicating the seriousness of the problem and the government's policy in regard to it.
Coupled with that there might be a statement from the minister as to what he is doing in regard to a serious situation in industry, as also in agriculture, under which men who have some particular knack or skill in certain types of production enlist before they are called for military service or before they are forced to leave; at any rate they leave these particular jobs, necessitating serious difficulties in replacement. New men undertaking work requiring this particular knack or expert ability have to be taught; it may be necessary to teach three or four to do one particular job in view of the possibility of future calls being made. I believe that generally across Canada for the past year or two this condition has been quite prevalent, and it is an annoying factor in war-time production. Certainly it has increased costs and lowered efficiency. I

War Appropriation
do not intend to go into the matter now in detail, but I would urge upon the Minister of Munitions and Supply and the Minister of Labour, as well as the Minister of Finance, that they give the house at the earliest possible moment a full and complete statement of their policy with respect to that situation. It would do much to raise or restore the confidence of the people and promote subscriptions to the victory loan, as well as ensure their approval of the house passing a bill of this size, $648 millions, in so short a time as we are asked to do it this afternoon.

speechtext:
I want to say a word
with regard to some observations of the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross). I do not propose at this time to go into the whole question of discharges from the army, because I am having a full statement prepared with regard to it; but in order that there may be no misapprehension I want the committee to understand now one or two features in connection with the matter.
Enlistments in the army, as everybody knows, have been to a considerable extent of men slightly older than the men of the last war. The younger men have gone into the air force. There has been a constant pressure on me from every direction-and that means industry, agriculture, and my colleague the Minister of Labour-to take in men who are perhaps not category A or A-l in order to give them a trial in the army. I have endeavoured to do my best, but we have seen to it that men have not been taken in below B-l except for certain special services. They have been put to a stiff training, some have been weeded out and these have gone back to industry.	*

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY   INTERIM APPROPRIATION
speechtext: Can a B-l man fight with a bayonet in hand-to-hand battle?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY   INTERIM APPROPRIATION
speechtext:
Certainly, and a B-2 man too. They have gone back to industry, and the result of that weed-out here has been that only six thousand out of all the tens of thousands who went overseas have been discharged overseas in this war. It may be that some men were taken into the army who should not have been admitted, but there has been this pressure of which I speak, and the charge is always made that the army is too "choosy" in connection with its men. We have met that situation as best we can. As I say, we have given them very stiff training. It must be remembered that this war will have lasted four years in September. Many of these men have been in the army a long time and have done a tremendous amount of heavy training, marching and all that sort of thing, which has had its effect on some of them.
72537-102J
With regard' to discharges generally, I am having a return made comparing them with discharges in other countries. With regard to the curve of discharges, I believe it will be found that the curve started coming down in September, 1942, and that the trend is gradually declining. But I do not want the committee or the country to get the idea that waste is being practised in the army in connection with these men. Every possible care is being taken to conserve our manpower to utilize what we have, and to see to it at the same time that men do not go overseas unless they are qualified in every way to carry out the duties and responsibilities which they will meet there. I want it to be understood by the committee. I think it will be found that the percentage of discharges does not vary much from the percentage of discharges in other countries.
Some reference was made, and I shall deal with it further when that war appropriation is made up, to the matter of waste in camps. I am not in a position to deal with general charges or suggestions of the kind. I am in a position to deal with any charge with regard to waste in any camp in Canada at any time. I have had this up before-cases in which individuals have written me about waste taking place in camps. In one case a public-spirited lady and her associates were extremely anxious to see that waste was eliminated. They had heard most alarming rumours with regard to the waste which was going on in one of our biggest camps in Canada. I wrote to her that I would arrange that they could go to the camp, if she would just let me know what day would be convenient. She wrote back and said no, she would not let me know, because everything would be all ready for them if she did, but she asked if I would give instructions to the commandant to receive them at any time they might come to the camp, which might not be for three months. Those instructions were given; she and her associates went to the camp, where they were shown from cellar to attic, figuratively speaking. They were taken to the dumps, the incinerators, the kitchens and the messes; and I think the best testimonial I have ever received as to the administration of that branch of the department came from that lady after this visit by herself and her associates. I am not saying conditions are always so good, but I mention this case in order to indicate that we endeavoured to run down these charges of waste in connection with the camps. That goes for salvage, as it goes for swill, garbage and everything of that kind. If the hon. member for Souris has any case he cares to mention with regard to waste in
War Appropriation

campa I invite him to do so, and I can assure him that I personally will see to it that the matter is gone into, that the facts are made known and that action is taken.

speechtext: I would like an answer from the Minister of Munitions and Supply to the suggestion that the members of this house be provided with a list of contracts awarded, so that we may be in a position to check up on these contracts, which we have not been able to do for the last year and a half.

Early in the war it was the practice of this department to publish such a list. We attempted to do it monthly, but the compilation required1 a great deal of work and, as my hon. friend will recall, we fell two or three months behind. There was objection from the services to publishing this information; we were told that for reasons of security it was not wise to do so. The British government also objected. They said it was not done in- England and should not be done here, and of course some of the contracts included in the lists were for British account. There were so many objections that we finally abandoned the practice. As a matter of fact the cost of compilation was growing from day to day, and at the time we stopped it the cost was something like $65,000 a year. I have no objection to resuming that practice if hon. members think it would be money well spent; for I believe the reasons of security are different to-day from w7hat they were at that time. It is just a question whether it is -worth the effort. As my hon. friend will appreciate, it

War Appropriation
requires quite a large staff, and it is difficult to keep the information up to date. The printing gets very much behind, particularly when parliament is sitting. My hon. friend will recall that the list became very voluminous. Perhaps one of the committees of the house could go through the list. We could make it available to a committee, which could select contracts which might be of interest to hon. members. If it is necessary to publish every contract down to $3.20 we can do so. I should be glad to have one of the committees study the question and advise the department what should be done. I assure the hon. member there is no desire to withhold information from this house.

speechtext: It is not a question of contracts for $3.20. If members of this house had available to them, in the office of the minister or elsewhere, a list of contracts for $10,000 or over, we then would be in a position to check up and scrutinize the accounts, which we are not able to do to-day. A large amount of money has been expended in my constituency in connection with the air force. I have no idea and no information as to what were the expenditures, when they were made or who got the money. I have heard criticism, not in my own constituency but in another nearby, in regard to airport purchases. Large sums of money in the estimates or in a resolution such as that before the committee to-day arc voted, but there is no real check thereof by parliament. The suggestion has been made that we might ask questions. That is impossible, having in mind the delay in answering questions dealing with the mobilization of man-power and the like, in connection with which we have to wait three or four weeks for the information. I do suggest that the minister should make available to the members of this house, not by publication if that is going to cost a great deal of money but certainly at least in his own office, a list of the contracts awarded from month to month, so that members of this house may in part at least discharge their responsibility of examining expenditures. I do ask the minister to give consideration to that suggestion; for as matters stand to-day it is impossible for us to discharge our responsibilities. We have no information as to what expenditures are being made, and without that information how can we carry out our duty to scrutinize critically the money that is spent? We are not discharging our responsibility unless the information is made available to us.
